extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, communications students, and business communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying one of Grunig & Hunt's four public relations models (press agentry, public information, two-way asymmetrical, two-way symmetrical) to design PR/communication strategies. Explains each model, their strengths and limitations, and when to use or combine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Agentry Model (Publicity model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation uses media manipulation to shape the narrative deceptively. Historically associated with P.T. Barnum and characterised by flamboyant tactics to garner attention (publicity stunts, press tours, exaggerated buzz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-way communication focused on persuasion and attention. Can generate initial interest in a product or event but is often perceived as self-serving and may not reflect an organisation’s genuine values or commitment to ethical conduct. Use when the immediate goal is visibility or buzz, but be aware of reputational and ethical risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Information Model
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation is practising one-way communication to disseminate information with little or no feedback from recipients. Focuses on disseminating accurate and objective information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linked to Ivy Lee’s early PR work; prioritises providing comprehensive, unbiased data to foster trust and credibility. Effective when the primary need is to inform stakeholders with facts and figures. Its limitation is the lack of engagement and limited effectiveness when audience perspectives and feedback matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Way Asymmetrical Model
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation engages in two-way communication to persuade and establish power structures. Incorporates persuasion and feedback to improve communications, relying on research and understanding of the target audience to craft tailored messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary goal is to influence public opinion while taking audience feedback into account. Improves audience engagement versus one-way models but still prioritises the organisation’s objectives over stakeholders’ needs. Useful when you need data-driven persuasion and message tailoring, but be mindful of ethical implications of privileging organisational aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Way Symmetrical Model
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation engages in two-way communication to find common ground and mutual benefits. Emphasises open, transparent communication and dialogue to understand each other’s perspectives, values, and concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes collaboration, trust, and long-term relationship building by seeking a balance between the interests of both parties. Presented as the most ethical and practical approach and the ‘‘gold standard’’ for contemporary PR practice, especially in interconnected and globalised contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence PR approach (objectives and corporate value focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public relations approach that focuses on objectives and corporate value creation; provides a management-theory basis for PR so it works well in sophisticated organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underlies the theory that PR should move beyond tactical tools to strategic management. The Excellence study concluded the two-way symmetrical model is most effective; also identifies testable variables to measure the quality of organisational relationships (i.e., relationship-focused evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual suitability / PR model selection guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when choosing a PR model: the organisation’s immediate goals (visibility, information dissemination, persuasion, relationship-building), ethical considerations, need for audience feedback, and available research on target publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: use press agentry to generate initial interest; use public information to disseminate facts and figures; use two-way asymmetrical when balancing persuasion and audience engagement; prefer two-way symmetrical for long-term trust and collaboration. Selection should weigh strengths and limitations of each model relative to stakeholder needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid approach recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: While two-way symmetrical is widely considered the most desirable approach, the other three models may still have their place in specific contexts and organisations should consider a hybrid approach that combines elements of each model as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexibility enables businesses to adapt to diverse and changing stakeholder needs while maintaining a commitment to honest and transparent communication. Use a hybrid mix to maximise effectiveness—for instance, combine publicity to launch interest with symmetrical dialogue for relationship maintenance.
